I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This is an
application for judicial review
[1]
.

[
2
]

The applicant seeks
an order quashing the October 2, 2019 decision of the Manitoba Human Rights
Commission (Commission), dismissing her complaint.  The complaint is that the
respondent discriminates against her, her family and other 2SLGBTQIA+
[2]

individuals in the provision of education by failing to ensure the kindergarten
to grade twelve curriculum and learning materials include gender identity and
sexual orientation.  The applicant also seeks an order directing the Commission
to reconsider the complaint.

[
3
]

Intervenor status
was granted to the Commission.  The Commission took no position in respect of
the merits of the application, limiting its submissions to explaining the
complaints process as well as the mandate, structure and role of the
Commission.

[
4
]

The key question
for me to decide is whether the Commission's decision to dismiss the complaint is
reasonable.  The applicant says, it is not.  The respondent says, it is.

[
5
]

For the following
reasons, I agree with the applicant.

II.     FACTS

[
6
]

The applicant
identifies as queer.  She is the parent of two children.  Her eldest daughter is
transgender and, during 2008 to 2009, attended first grade at a Manitoba public
school.  In her complaint to the Commission, the applicant states her eldest
daughter experienced transphobia as well has homophobia; the latter because her
parents are queer.  These phobias manifested themselves in the form of
bullying, aggravated by educators being ill-equipped and/or unable to deal with
the situation.
[3]

[
7
]

In response, the applicant
removed her child from public school, opting instead to home-school.  Despite
being at home, the applicant continued to access the respondent's curriculum so
as to know and achieve grade-specific learning outcomes.  The applicant
alleges, among other things, the curriculum prescribed by the respondent fails
to reference diversity of gender, sexuality and family; an omission made worse
by discretion vested in school divisions and teachers to determine whether, and
to what extent, to include such diversity in their lesson plans.

[
8
]

Because of the
matters referred to in paragraphs 6 and 7 of these reasons, on July 7, 2017,
the applicant filed the complaint with the Commission.  As noted in my
introduction, she alleges the respondent
discriminates against her, her family
and other 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals in the provision of education by failing to
ensure the kindergarten to grade twelve curriculum and learning materials
include gender identity and sexual orientation in contravention of
section 13

of
The
Human Rights Code
, C.C.S.M. c. H175 (
Code
).
That section prohibits discrimination with respect to, among other things, any
service available to the public or to a section of the public, unless
bona
fide
and reasonable cause exists for the discrimination.
Section 9
of the
Code

defines "discrimination" to include the differential treatment of an
individual or group on the basis of, among other things, sex, gender identity
or sexual orientation or on the basis of that individual's or group's
association with another individual or group whose identity or membership is
determined by those same characteristics.

[
9
]

The respondent filed
its response to the complaint on August 22, 2017.  Over the next two years, the
Commission's investigation team investigated the complaint and, on July 22,
2019, submitted a forty-page Investigation Report (fourteen pages of analysis,
twenty-five pages of evidentiary/documentary summaries, one page recommendation),
ultimately recommending to the Board of Commissioners (Board) that it refer the
complaint to adjudication as that would further the objectives of the
Code
.

Section 29(3)
of the
Code
specifically provides:

Adjudication or
prosecution

29(3)
If a complaint is not settled, terminated or dismissed and the
Commission is satisfied that additional proceedings in respect of the complaint
would further the objectives of this
Code
or assist the Commission in
discharging its responsibilities under this Code, the Commission shall

(a)   request the chief adjudicator to designate a member of
the adjudication panel to adjudicate the complaint; or

(b)   recommend that the minister commence a prosecution for
an alleged contravention of the
Code
.

[
10
]

The Investigation Report was shared with
the parties with an invitation to respond.  Written responses from the
applicant and respondent were received by the Commission on or about September
9, 2019.

[
11
]

On October 2, 2019, the Board dismissed
[4]

the complaint, communicating its decision and reasons to the parties, in
writing, by a one-page letter dated October 18, 2019.  The most material
paragraphs of the letter state:

The Board did not
accept the investigator's recommendation to request an adjudicator to conduct a
public hearing of the complaint.  Rather, the Board decided to dismiss the
complaint under section 29(1)(c) of the [
Code
].

While the Board underscored the importance
of ensuring that Manitoba's curriculum fosters the inclusion of all students
and families, upon review of the evidence, the Board did not find sufficient
evidence to conclude on a balance of probabilities that the [r]espondent's
curriculum, in and of itself, contributes to the creation of a discriminatory
learning environment for the [complainant's] children, or other Manitoba
students and families.  In making its decision, the Board relied on evidence
regarding the broad nature of the [r]espondent's curriculum framework, and
considered evidence which indicates that the [r]respondent's curriculum
framework, along with other supplementary policy and learning materials,
support the delivery of an education that is responsive to the diversity of
Manitoba communities.  The Board also considered the broader legislative
context within which provincial curriculum standards operate, which support
inclusive learning environments, mandate that school divisions have in place
diversity policies and abide by the [
Code
].

While there is no reconsideration process
under the [
Code
], you may apply to the Court of Queen's Bench for
a judicial review of the Commission's decision….

[
12
]

The applicant filed this application
for judicial review on November 21, 2019.

III.    STANDARD
OF REVIEW

[
13
]

The parties and the intervenor take the
position the presumptive reasonableness standard of review applies in this case
as the conditions necessary to rebut the application of a reasonableness
standard are not present.  See
Canada (Minister of Citizenship and
Immigration) v. Vavilov
,
2019 SCC 65 (CanLII)
, at paras.
23–3
2 and
33–5
2
.

[
14
]

I agree with their position.

IV.     DECISION

A.      Framework
of a Reasonableness Review

[
15
]

In
Vavilov
, the Supreme
Court of Canada set out a framework for conducting a reasonableness review.  To
paraphrase:

·

The onus is on the applicant to establish
unreasonableness (para. 100).

·

The reviewing court should not ask how
it
would
have decided the issue—the question is whether the applicant has demonstrated
the decision is unreasonable (paras. 75 and 85).

·

The starting point is judicial restraint (para. 75).
Reasons are not to be assessed by a standard of perfection (para. 91).

·

Where there are written reasons, a principled approach
to reasonableness review requires the court to begin by examining those reasons
in the context of the record to understand the reasoning process (para. 84).

·

There is a spectrum of decision makers including,
among others, specialized tribunals (the case here), independent regulatory
bodies, and ministers.  Their decisions will vary in nature and impact.
(para. 88)

·

Reasonableness is a "single standard"
(paras. 89–90).  The question of what is reasonable can be addressed by asking,
first, whether there is a failure of rationality internal to the reasoning
process
[5]

(a decision must be both justifiable and justified by sufficiently transparent
and intelligible reasons), and second, whether the decision is untenable given
the particular legal and factual context.  However, there is no need to
categorize types of failures.  (paras. 85–87, 99 and 101–104)

·

In respect of the second question, there is no "checklist"
for evaluating legal and factual contexts shaping a reasonableness review.
That said, some of the more common reference points are:  the governing
statutory scheme; other relevant statutory or common law; the principles of
statutory interpretation; the evidence before the decision maker and facts of
which the decision maker may take notice; the submissions of the parties; the
past practices and decisions of the administrative body; and the potential
impact of the decision on the individual to whom it applies.  The applicability
and importance of these or any other elements may vary with each case.  (para.
106)

B.      Is
the Commission's decision reasonable?

[
16
]

After considering
the parties' submissions in the context of the
Vavilov
framework,
I find the Commission's decision is not reasonable.  I reach this conclusion
mindful of the judicial restraint and deference owed to the Commission and its
role as described in the
Code
and case law:

•

By section 29 of the

Code
,
the Commission serves a gatekeeper function in
respect to which complaints are referred to adjudication.  See
Korsch v.
Human Rights Commission (Man.) et al.
,
2012 MBCA 108 (CanLII)
, at para.

10
.  This function has been compared to that of a judge at a preliminary
inquiry—its duty is to determine if an inquiry is warranted in light of the
evidence.  The threshold is low.  See
Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg
Inc. v. Metaser et al.
,
2013 MBQB 303 (CanLII)
, at para.
24
.

•

The Commission is
an independent and specialized tribunal, expert in its processes, procedures,
and law in the area of its decision making.
See
Jewish Community Campus
of Winnipeg Inc.
at para.
18
.

•

The Commission is
granted broad discretion when determining if it is "satisfied that
additional proceedings … would further the objectives of [the
Code
]
or assist the Commission in discharging its responsibilities under [the
Code
]".
See section 29(3);
Northern Regional Health Authority v. Manitoba Human
Rights Commission et al
,
2017 MBCA 98 (CanLII)
, at paras.
74–76
.

•

The investigator who
prepares the investigation report does so as an extension of the Commission,
not independent of it.  The report is prepared
for
the Commission at its
request.  See
Bell Canada v. Communications, Energy and Paperworkers Union
of Canada
,
1998 CanLII 8700 (FCA)
,
[1998] F.C.J. No. 1609 (QL)
, at para.
44
(C.A.)
.  In the
case where the Commission adopts the investigator's report and provides no
additional reasons, the investigator's report constitutes the Commission's
reasons.  See
David v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2007 FC 887
(CanLII)
, at para.
5
.

[
17
]

As is often the
case, at times basic principles may require some nuance when applying them.
For example, the authorities also suggest:

•

The Commission's dismissal
of a complaint at the screening stage may add to the seriousness of the
decision.  See
Johnstone v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2007 FC 36
(CanLII)
, at para.
13
;
Sketchley v. Canada (Attorney General)
,

2004 FC 1151 (CanLII)
, at para.
51
(appeal dismissed)
.

•

The Commission's dismissal
of a complaint without convincing reasons and contrary to the findings and
recommendation of the investigator warrants a particularly careful review.
See

Johnstone
at para.
13
.

[
18
]

Moving from the
role of the Commission to the particular complaint, there can be little doubt
the consequences of its dismissal are of significance to the applicant and
those sharing her concern.  Dismissal ends the matter then and there.  The
question of whether the respondent
discriminates against the applicant, her family and other
2SLGBTQIA+ individuals in the provision of education will not be adjudicated.
Without commenting on the merits of the complaint, judicial notice can be taken
of the prevalence in contemporary public discourse of issues relating to gender
identity and sexual orientation.

[
19
]

The consequences of
the dismissal coupled with the lengthy Investigation Report recommending
adjudication inevitably caused the applicant to question the adequacy of the
Commission's very brief reasons.  While I agree the role of the Commission is as
described in paragraph 16 of these reasons and that deference is owed to it, I also
agree with the statements from
Johnstone
and
Sketchley

referenced in paragraph
17
of these reasons.  Here, where the Commission's own
investigator performed a lengthy analysis (based on what they describe as
evidence (pages 15 to 35) and documents (pages 36 to 39)), recommending
adjudication that was then rejected by a majority of the Commission, "convincing"
reasons should be provided.  When I say "convincing", I am not
suggesting the reasons need to, or should be long, or that every point raised
by the investigator or the complainant need be addressed.  However, as
noted in

Vavilov
, the decision should be justifiable and justified.  If
the right to judicial review is to have meaning, an applicant should be able to
understand, from the face of the decision, why their complaint was rejected.

[
20
]

In the facts of
this case, the Commission's decision is lacking.  It may well be justifiable but,
objectively viewed, it is not sufficiently justified by transparent reasons.

[
21
]

The Commission dismisses
the complaint, relying on the statutorily prescribed ground of insufficient
evidence to substantiate the alleged contravention of the
Code

(
section 29(1)
(c)).  It proceeds to refer to categories of evidence upon which
it purportedly relied but, in my view, fails to provide meaningful examples.  The
rationale and import of the limiting language "in and of itself" used
in reference to the respondent's curriculum also lacks clarity.  When read
against the backdrop of the record, the decision resembles those decisions
found to be unreasonable on the ground they merely repeat statutory language and/or
fail to convey the decision maker's reasoning on critical points (see
footnote 5).

[
22
]

The applicant has
established, on a balance of probabilities, the Commission's decision is
unreasonable and should be quashed.

[
23
]

I direct the
Commission to reconsider this complaint.  The Commission may well reach the
same conclusion.  I have not based my reasonableness conclusion on the decision
being untenable given the legal and factual context.  However, the reasons in
support of the decision should provide the reader examples of not only the
category of evidence upon which it relies but also the evidence itself.  As
well, if, by using the phrase "in and of itself" in reference to the
curriculum, the Commission intends to connote a specific interpretation of the
relevant statutes and regulations, that too should be briefly articulated and
why.

V.      CONCLUSION

[
24
]

The application is
granted with costs to the applicant payable on a party and party scale in
accordance with the tariff in the Manitoba,
Court of Queen's Bench Rules
.
In the event the parties cannot agree on the amount of costs or the form of
order, they should come back before me.

_________________________J.

[1]
This application was argued at the same
time as the application filed in Queen's Bench File No. CI 19-01-24587
(McHale et al. v. Government of Manitoba – Manitoba Education and
Training), which, notwithstanding different applicants, raised the same issues
and requested the same relief.  But for the description of the applicants, and
some facts giving rise to their particular complaint, the materials filed in
the applications, including the record, mirror each other.

[2]
2SLGBTQIA+ is an acronym that stands for Two-Spirit,
Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Questioning, Intersex, Asexual,
and additional sexual orientations and gender identities.

[3]
For example, the child's gender identity
was not discussed with her classmates to address the bullying because of the
school division's position that such a discussion was not age appropriate.

[4]
The redacted minutes of the meeting
indicate three Board members voted to not dismiss the complaint.

[5]
Among the several illustrations of failures of internal
rationality noted by the Supreme Court of Canada were:  when reasons merely
repeat statutory language, summarize arguments made, and then state peremptory
conclusions, and when reasons, read in conjunction with the record, do not make
it possible to understand the decision maker's reasoning on a critical point.
